title: Monotonicity in T of the tight k-unit IID prophet ratio
short_statement: For the i.i.d. prophet inequality accepting up to $k$ of $T$ values, an LP captures the tight online-to-offline ratio. Numerically the ratio decreases in $T$; the conjecture is to prove this monotonicity for general $k$, which would fully characterize the tight $k$-unit IID prophet guarantee.
open_problem: Show that for each fixed $k$, $\mathrm{val}(k,T)$ is decreasing in $T$ (more arrivals make the gambler's task relatively harder). For $k=1$ this monotonicity was established by Correa et al.
background: The i.i.d. prophet inequality is one of the cleanest models in online selection. A decision maker observes $T$ independent draws from a known common distribution and must decide online which values to keep. In the $k$-unit version, at most $k$ values may be accepted, so the model interpolates between the classical single-choice prophet inequality and online resource allocation with a homogeneous capacity. The benchmark is the offline prophet, who sees all $T$ draws and keeps the best $k$. For $k=1$, the tight i.i.d. ratio is the Hill-Kertz constant, approximately $0.745$, and the underlying finite-horizon values are known to decrease to that limit. For larger $k$, Jiang, Ma, and Zhang show that the relevant tight ratio can be represented by an LP, but a simple structural fact remains missing: for fixed $k$, does the worst-case ratio decrease as the number of periods $T$ grows? A proof would turn a computationally defined finite-horizon family into a clean characterization of the tight $k$-unit i.i.d. prophet guarantee.
full_statement: Consider the IID prophet inequality with $T$ values and capacity $k$: T values arrive i.i.d. from a distribution $\mathbf F$, and the gambler may accept up to $k$ of them online, comparing against the offline optimum. Let $\mathrm{val}(k,T)=\inf_{\mathbf F}\mathrm{ONL}/\mathrm{OFF}$ be the tight competitive ratio (online versus offline) for given $k$ and $T$, captured by a known LP (the LP of the notes without the normalization constraint). \textbf{Open:} Show that for each fixed $k$, $\mathrm{val}(k,T)$ is decreasing in $T$ (more arrivals make the gambler's task relatively harder). For $k=1$ this monotonicity was established by Correa et al. (2017); the general $k$ case is open. Proving it would fully characterize the tight $k$-unit IID prophet guarantee.
known_results: For $k=1$, Hill and Kertz identified the limiting i.i.d. prophet constant and later work by Correa, Foncea, Hoeksma, Oosterwijk, and Vredeveld gave the tight finite-horizon interpretation used in posted-price mechanisms. Jiang, Ma, and Zhang characterize the tight multi-unit ratio relative to the standard LP/fluid relaxation and show that Alaei's widely used $1-1/\sqrt{k+3}$ guarantee is not tight for $k>1$. The open monotonicity question is about the online-to-offline finite-horizon ratio captured by the LP from Will Ma's notes: numerical evidence suggests $\mathrm{val}(k,T)$ decreases in $T$ for every fixed $k$, but no proof is known beyond $k=1$.

progress.summary: No general-$k$ proof of monotonicity is known in the site sources. The problem remains a finite-dimensional inequality/LP-structure question rather than a modelling question.

counterexample_rationale: For fixed small $k$ and $T$, the conjecture can be stress-tested by solving the finite LPs and searching for a monotonicity violation. A counterexample would likely be a finite certificate.
alphaevolve_rationale: An evolutionary or symbolic-search loop could look for dual certificates, reductions between adjacent horizons, or finite counterexamples. A final proof would still need a rigorous LP or coupling argument.

literature.synthesis: The single-item i.i.d. prophet inequality has a long optimal-stopping history, with the Hill-Kertz constant giving the limiting worst-case ratio and later algorithmic work connecting the same constant to posted prices. Multi-unit prophet inequalities became central because they are used as subroutines for ad allocation, appointment scheduling, and revenue-management relaxations. Jiang, Ma, and Zhang show that the tight multi-unit guarantee in Alaei's LP setting is strictly better than the classical bound, and their analysis supplies the LP objects behind Will Ma's course-note open problem. What is missing is a monotonicity theorem in the horizon $T$. Such a theorem would let one identify the worst case by passing to the infinite-horizon limit, rather than treating each $T$ separately.

reviewed.result: Characterizes tight guarantees for multi-unit prophet inequalities relative to the standard LP/fluid benchmark and improves online stochastic knapsack guarantees.

reviewed.ref: Jose Correa, Patricio Foncea, Ruben Hoeksma, Tim Oosterwijk, Tjark Vredeveld, 'Posted Price Mechanisms for a Random Stream of Customers', EC 2017
reviewed.result: Gives the tight single-item i.i.d. prophet/posting-price guarantee and finite-horizon structure used as the $k=1$ analogue.

reviewed.ref: Theodore P. Hill, Robert P. Kertz, 'Comparisons of stop rule and supremum expectations of i.i.d. random variables', Annals of Probability 1982
reviewed.result: Classical source for the limiting i.i.d. prophet constant.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Good attack routes include deriving an explicit dual for the finite-horizon LP, proving a horizon-extension coupling from $T$ to $T+1$, or finding a total-positivity/majorization property of the worst-case distribution. A computational agent should first reproduce small-$k$ LP values and inspect dual variables for a pattern.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A correct proof must compare the exact worst-case ratios for adjacent horizons at fixed $k$, not just show monotonicity for a particular policy or distribution family. A counterexample must include enough numerical precision and preferably rational LP data so the strict violation can be independently certified.
